On failure the backoff runs 30 seconds to 10 minutes. The 90 seconds is not arbitrary: it used to be 30 minutes, and against a 1-hour bundle whose boundary term sat ~55 minutes out, that single constant meant **an admin who flipped a rule in the console waited 24–36 minutes for it to take effect on every surface at once** — IDE hooks, CLI shims, the AI proxy and the browser extension all read the one bundle. The cost of the change is fetch volume (~40 polls/hour/endpoint instead of ~2), most of which are reads: the Backend reuses the stored bundle when the policy has not changed and re-signs only on a real change.

The honest shape is that enforcement continues from the last-known policy forever, with a Debug-level log until ten minutes and a re-warn only every fifteen minutes after that. The document's own evidence rule demands that a control which cannot reach a decision says what it does; §8 says it for the endpoint's *activation* path but not for its *delivery* path.

An admin could tighten policy, watch it save, and have endpoints silently ignore it.' :343 `aiPolicyStaleAfter = 10 * time.Minute`; :347 `aiPolicyStaleReWarnEvery = 15 * time.Minute`; :353-360 `policyStaleness`; :362+ `freshnessHealth`. omissions.proposedText: Add to §8.4: "**When the policy fetch fails.** Nothing changes about enforcement: the last-known policy keeps being served, which is correct — failing open on a backend blip would be worse. What changes is only visibility, and it changes late. Below ten minutes the failure is a Debug log and nothing else. At ten minutes the endpoint marks itself stale, escalates the log and raises a flag on `/health` and `doctor`; after that it re-warns only every fifteen minutes so a long outage leaves a breadcrumb rather than a flood. An endpoint that has *never* fetched successfully but is serving a disk-seeded copy counts as stale from the start — that is the daemon-restarted-while-broken case. reorganisation:
Three structural changes, in order of value.

(1) **§8.1 needs a fourth paragraph, and it must come before the folding rules, not after.** As written, §8.1 runs authoring → transaction → folding → default materialisation, and every step reads as "the administrator decides". The serve-time malicious floor breaks that and must be stated where a reader forms the mental model, not buried in §13's fail-closed inventory. Put it immediately after the transaction paragraph: the floor is the last thing that happens between the console and the wire, so it belongs at the end of the write story and the start of the read story. The `destructive-rm` consequence goes with it as its own paragraph — it is the only place in the document where a named detector class, a floor minimum, and a customer-visible outcome can be joined up in three sentences.

(2) **§8.4 is doing two jobs and should be split.** Its first half (strict parse, three shapes, thirteen — actually twelve — refusal reasons) is the *verification* contract, which is pure and testable and mirrored byte-for-byte in a cross-repo corpus. Its second half (postures, containment, cache lifetimes) is the *operational* state machine, which is stateful, environment-dependent, and where every measured incident in this chapter actually happened. Split into "8.4 Verification: what the endpoint checks" and "8.5 Posture, containment and freshness: what the endpoint does", pushing the version gate to 8.6. The refusal-reason list should become a table with three columns — slug, when it fires, what the endpoint does next — because as a prose list it hides that two different failures share `untrusted-root` and that six of the twelve only fire under V2 compatibility.

(3) **§10.2's two-lane framing is right and should be applied to §10.1 too.** §10.1 currently mixes the server-side chain (per-org sequence, versioned hash, advisory lock) with the endpoint-side spool (WAL, ack validation, watermark) in two paragraphs, and they have completely different failure modes and different owners. Split them: "10.1 The server-side chain" and "10.2 The endpoint spool and its acknowledgement", moving prompt text to 10.3. The eleven ack refusals then have somewhere to live as a list, and the deploy-order hazard (an agent carrying the signed-floor check against an older Backend stalls delivery fleet-wide while looking like a healthy backlog) gets a home — right now it has nowhere to go and is absent from the document entirely.

One smaller note: §9 is a single un-subsectioned block covering enrolment, request signing, server modes, storage, the reinstall brick and the heartbeat. It is the longest unbroken run in Part I and it carries five of this review's corrections. Four subsections — enrolment and the device credential; request signing on the wire; storage and measurement; the reinstall brick and what is still open — would let each carry its own failure mode without the paragraph-per-topic compression that produced the "five headers"/"four validations" undercounts.
